vignette: Kevin, a 27-year-old African American male who works as an Uber driver, has been struggling with the aftermath of physical abuse he experienced at the hands of his caregiver during childhood. This trauma has left him feeling profoundly changed and disconnected from both himself and his community. One day, while driving through a busy city street, Kevin noticed the texture of the leather steering wheel. The roughness was reminiscent of the coarse fabric that his abuser often wore. Suddenly, he felt a wave of panic rising within him. He turned up the radio loudly to distract himself from the memory and the increasing sense of danger. This pattern had become a familiar cycle: the specific triggers, such as tactile sensations or sounds like footsteps behind him, would ignite a visceral fear that he could barely control. Kevin's hypervigilance had become his constant companion. He was always on guard, constantly scanning his surroundings for any potential threat. Even when others assured him he was safe, it was impossible for him to believe them. This pervasive sense of danger led Kevin to engage in risky behaviors, such as speeding or taking dangerous routes through the city, as if he needed to prove to himself that he could handle anything that came his way. The physical sensations were just one aspect; the emotional landscape was equally challenging. Kevin had come to believe that he was permanently changed for the worse and that his body continued to react as if he were still in danger, even when he was safe at home or driving through the city streets. This belief made it nearly impossible for him to connect with others on a deep level; intimacy felt too risky, and he avoided forming close relationships. He found solace in distracting himself from these thoughts by taking drugs, which offered temporary relief but exacerbated his sense of disconnection. The negative appraisals that Kevin held about himself and his body reinforced the maladaptive strategies he used to cope with his distress. His belief in permanent damage made it difficult for him to trust anyone or anything, leading him to isolate further and engage more frequently in risky behaviors as a form of self-medication. This cycle only deepened his sense of isolation and mistrust. Kevin's community connections had suffered significantly due to these coping mechanisms. He no longer participated in cultural events or social gatherings that once brought him joy and a sense of belonging. The loss of this connection further fueled the negative appraisals he held about himself, creating a self-reinforcing loop where his maladaptive strategies and heightened threat perceptions fed into one another. It was only after a particularly harrowing incident while driving late at night-when footsteps behind him triggered intense panic-that Kevin realized he needed to seek help. The fear had become too consuming, and the isolation too profound. He was certain that something had to change before it was too late. Despite his fears of re-engaging with others and being vulnerable again, Kevin was hopeful that therapy could offer a path toward healing and reclaiming a sense of safety and connection. In seeking help, Kevin hoped to break free from the cycle of avoidance and hypervigilance that had dominated his life for so long. He understood that the road ahead would be challenging but believed it was worth it to regain a sense of trust in himself and others.
